strengths: The main contribution is best assessed as Theory/Foundational: the attention-dependent Jacobian bound and refined softmax spectral bound are more central than benchmark performance. These results could be useful without achieving state-of-the-art robustness.

Theorem 3 explicitly separates the attention matrix, softmax Jacobians, input norms, and projection weights. Theorem 4 provides a readily computable bound using ordered probabilities, capturing the vanishing softmax derivative near one-hot distributions that a constant bound misses.

JaSMin translates the theoretical analysis into a practical regularizer without changing the inference architecture. The maximum/mean aggregation and ratio variants receive substantial hyperparameter exploration.

The experiments provide encouraging evidence: selected softmax bounds closely approximate measured norms, and CIFAR-100 PGD4 accuracy improves from 12.91% to 19.58%, with clean accuracy decreasing from 90.9% to 89.1%. Comparisons with Specformer and attention visualizations help connect the analysis to vision models.
weaknesses: The robustness evaluation is insufficiently strong to establish the practical claims. PGD uses only four steps, and the reported ten-step AutoAttack departs from the standard evaluation without adequately specifying the configuration. Longer attacks, restarts, convergence checks, and standard AutoAttack are needed. The substantial gap between PGD2 and AA2 accuracy makes this concern particularly consequential.

The manuscript repeatedly conflates pointwise Jacobian norms with neighborhood Lipschitz constants and whole-network robustness. Theorem 3 bounds the Jacobian at X; a finite-radius bound requires controlling its supremum throughout the neighborhood. Figure 4 also excludes patch embedding despite describing the whole model. Moreover, the theory uses Euclidean norms while attacks use the infinity norm, without establishing the corresponding quantitative connection.

Small softmax Jacobian norms do not alone imply small attention or network Lipschitz constants. Equation (3) retains input and weight factors and the spectral norm of P; nearly one-hot rows attending to the same token can yield a spectral norm approaching sqrt(N). Thus, the claim that uniform or categorical attention necessarily gives a small model Lipschitz constant is overstated. JaSMin does not directly control all these other factors.

The evidence does not isolate the benefit of the proposed spectral surrogate from simpler distribution regularizers, such as attention entropy or concentration penalties. Evaluation covers only ViT-B fine-tuning on CIFAR-10/100, lacks repeated-run uncertainty, and shows mixed tradeoffs: on CIFAR-10, the k=0 mean variant slightly worsens both PGD and AA accuracy. Figure 6 demonstrates improvement over prior bounds, but the full attention bound remains substantially above the measured Jacobian norm.

Several theoretical and reproducibility details need correction or completion. Theorem 4 divides by an eigenvector component without handling repeated probabilities or zero components explicitly, and uses an undefined g_n. Appendix B states an interlacing direction without the required sign restriction on the rank-one perturbation. Training omits the learning-rate value and checkpoint adaptation details for patch size four, and the claimed lightweight overhead is not measured. These are mostly repairable, but matter for a theory-centered submission.

strengths: Theorem 3 makes attention-distribution dependence explicit in a tractable bound on the self-attention Jacobian. This is a useful theoretical refinement over bounds based only on input and weight norms, with potential relevance to understanding vision-transformer stability.

Theorem 4 provides an inexpensive softmax-Jacobian bound using the two largest probabilities. It captures both diffuse and nearly one-hot distributions, and Figures 2–3 demonstrate close agreement with exact norms for the selected attention heads.

JaSMin preserves the standard attention operation. Experiments include a substantial hyperparameter sweep against Specformer and show promising improvements: on CIFAR-100, one configuration increases PGD4 accuracy from 12.91% to 19.58%, while clean accuracy decreases from 90.9% to 89.1%. The appendices provide derivations and additional results.
weaknesses: The adversarial evaluation is insufficiently strong to establish the central robustness claim. Section 5 uses only four PGD steps and describes AutoAttack as using ten steps, without adequately specifying the modified suite, restarts, or convergence checks. Longer attacks and standard AutoAttack are needed to determine whether the gains persist. The large gap between PGD2 and AA2 results further motivates this verification.

The manuscript overextends its pointwise analysis. Theorem 3 bounds a Jacobian at X; a finite-neighborhood Lipschitz bound requires controlling its supremum throughout that neighborhood. Furthermore, reducing the softmax factor alone does not control the other factors in Equation 3. Nearly one-hot attention can still have an attention-matrix spectral norm approaching sqrt(N) when rows attend to the same token. Thus, the introduction's claim that a small model Lipschitz constant must hold in the identified distributional regimes is not established.

The evidence for whole-network sensitivity reduction is narrower than claimed. Figure 4 is captioned as measuring the whole model's Jacobian, but Section 5 explicitly removes patch embedding. These pointwise measurements therefore do not establish sensitivity to image-space perturbations or a neighborhood robustness guarantee. Figure 6 also compares bounds on one regularized checkpoint rather than demonstrating a before/after reduction; despite improving substantially over prior bounds, many reported log10 bound values remain roughly one to two orders of magnitude above the corresponding numerical Jacobian norms.

The practical advantages are inconsistent and insufficiently isolated. In Table 2, the mean k=0 configuration slightly worsens PGD2, PGD4, and AA2 relative to the baseline. Appendix Table 4 reports Specformer AA2 accuracy of 4.38%, exceeding several highlighted JaSMin configurations. The broad claim of outperforming Specformer across robust metrics needs qualification through matched clean-accuracy comparisons, repeated runs, and comparisons with simpler attention-distribution penalties. Evaluation on one architecture and two closely related datasets leaves generality uncertain.

Several details limit reproducibility and theoretical precision. The training description omits the initial learning rate and how ImageNet-pretrained patch embeddings are adapted to patch size four; runtime and memory overhead are not measured despite the lightweight claim. Theorem 4 uses an undefined g_n and its proof divides by an eigenvector coordinate without handling zero coordinates or repeated probabilities. These proof issues appear repairable, but should be resolved. Equation 11 also writes singular values of an attention row where the softmax Jacobian appears intended.

strengths: The main contribution is best assessed as Theory/Foundational: the paper develops attention-dependent Jacobian bounds, with JaSMin as an application. Under this assessment, the theoretical insight matters more than achieving state-of-the-art adversarial accuracy.

Theorem 3 exposes the contribution of attention probabilities to self-attention sensitivity, rather than relying only on input and weight norms. Theorem 4 provides a useful, inexpensive bound based on the two largest softmax probabilities, correctly capturing the vanishing Jacobian near one-hot distributions.

The theory is accompanied by informative empirical checks. Figures 2–3 show that the softmax bound closely approximates measured norms for the selected heads, while Figure 6 demonstrates substantially tighter attention bounds than the compared alternatives.

JaSMin preserves ordinary dot-product attention and produces useful empirical improvements. For example, on CIFAR-100, the k=10 mean variant improves PGD4 accuracy from 12.91% to 19.58%, although clean accuracy decreases from 90.9% to 89.1%. The appendix includes a substantial hyperparameter sweep.

Overall, the distribution-sensitive analysis and its practical regularizer provide a sufficiently interesting contribution for a narrow acceptance recommendation, provided the claims are calibrated to the evidence.
weaknesses: The robustness evaluation is insufficiently strong to establish the broader robustness claims. PGD uses only four steps, and AutoAttack is described as using ten steps without adequately specifying how its components were modified. Converged attacks, restarts, and a standard AutoAttack evaluation are needed to establish whether the improvements persist. Reported AutoAttack accuracies remain low, and several improvements involve appreciable clean-accuracy losses.

The manuscript sometimes conflates a pointwise Jacobian norm with a Lipschitz constant over a finite neighborhood. Theorem 3 bounds the former; a finite-radius bound requires controlling its terms throughout that neighborhood. Moreover, a small softmax Jacobian alone does not guarantee small attention or network sensitivity: the bound also contains input norms, weight norms, and the attention-matrix norm. These qualifications weaken the claimed explanation of training stability and robustness.

Figure 4 is described as measuring the whole model's Jacobian, but the experiments explicitly remove patch embedding. This measures sensitivity to intermediate representations rather than input images. Because the omitted transformation can affect both scale and sensitivity, this experiment does not establish the claimed reduction in the full image-to-output Jacobian.

Some theoretical details require correction. Theorem 4's proof divides by an eigenvector coordinate without handling zero coordinates or repeated probabilities. Its statement also uses an undefined g_n. The discussion following Proposition 1 incorrectly says any distribution uniform over p≥k tokens attains g_1/g_k=1: for exactly k nonzero equal probabilities, the ratio is k/(k−1). These appear repairable, but precision is particularly important for a theory-centered submission.

The experiments do not isolate the value of the proposed spectral surrogate from simpler attention-distribution regularizers, such as entropy or maximum-probability penalties. Evaluation is limited to ViT-B fine-tuning on CIFAR-10/100; the ImageNet analysis is diagnostic rather than a robustness experiment. Multiple seeds and uncertainty estimates are also absent.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence are incomplete. The exact pretraining checkpoint and adaptation to four-pixel patches, learning-rate value, attack step sizes and restarts, and model-selection protocol need clarification. The 'lightweight' claim lacks comparative training-time and memory measurements; total GPU hours do not establish per-step overhead.
